pages.text: 7 Classic Food Experiences to Try in Marseille | National Geographic TRAVEL 7 Classic Food Experiences to Try in Marseille From bouillabaisse to panisse, distinctive dishes help to define France’s largest and most vibrant port city. Here’s where to seek out the best flavours of the sunny south. Maison Empereur in Marseille is an Aladdin’s cave of hardware and homewares. Andrew Hasson, Alamy Stock By Sarah Barrell Published November 14, 2026 This article was produced by National Geographic Traveller (UK). Elegant and edgy — and offering a distinctively warm southern welcome — Marseille is a place where an increasing number of food-focused travellers are making pilgrimages. Come for the pastis — the anise-flavoured spirit that sings of Provencal summers, invented in the city in 1932 by native Paul Ricard. And stay for the unique blend of North African and French flavours found on local bistro menus and in street snacks such as panisse (chickpea fritters) and food truck pizza — also born here in the 1960s. Don’t leave without sampling bouillabaisse, the nation-defining seafood soup with humble roots in the port city’s fishing communities. 1. Shop Like an Emperor Head to warren-like emporium Maison Empereur on the central Rue des Récolettes, established in 1827. Its creaky floors, set over two storeys, are packed with every imaginable kitchen gadget, from traditional fluted copper canelé moulds to an arsenal of Japanese sushi knives, plus local delicacies like olive oils, fleur de sel sea salt and herby syrups that showcase flavours of the French south. 2. Make the most of summer by seeking out the ones that still fly under the radar. From France's mountainous Mercantour National Park to sand dunes in Poland's Słowiński National Park, Europe's wealth of national parks has a landscape for every traveller. Westend61, Getty Images By Sarah Baxter Published May 18, 2026 This article was produced by National Geographic Traveller (UK). At the last count, Europe had well over 400 national parks, representing a vast diversity of landscapes and habitats — from the forest-clad mountains of the north to the coastal wetlands of the south. Within that range, there are huge number of surprises — parks that offer wholly unique experiences within their boundaries and whose trails see less footfall than the big-hitters. Whether you want to canoe between islands on Finland’s largest lake, wander enormous sand dunes in the middle of Poland or explore ancient forests in the Canary Islands, there’s a national park for you. 1. pages.description: Music, dance and ancient traditions take centre stage at Latin America’s most spectacular festivals, offering an unforgettable insight into the region’s rich cultural heritage.
pages.text: 7 of Latin America's Unmissable Festivals | National Geographic By Daniel Stables Published August 26, 2026 This article was produced by National Geographic Traveller (UK). Festivals are woven into the fabric of life throughout Latin America — from the Bolivian Altiplano and the Peruvian Andes to the far reaches of Easter Island. They’re events where communities come together to celebrate faith, heritage and identity, often blending Indigenous traditions with influences brought by European colonisers centuries ago. And for travellers, they’re an opportunity to experience local culture at its most vivid. Streets fill with music and dance, as performers parade through cities, towns and village squares, while age-old rituals are brought to life before cheering crowds. Here are seven of the best. 1. Oruro Carnival , Bolivia When: Most events in the six days leading up to Ash Wednesday (4-10 February 2027) Why: For demonic dances in the high Andes Bolivia’s Oruro Carnival has to be one of the most eye-catching celebrations in Latin America. Originally an Indigenous festival of the Uru people, it centred on a pilgrimage to the sacred mountains surrounding Oruro, where participants prayed for protection from deities associated with toads, lizards and snakes. When the Spanish arrived, they blended these traditions with Christian beliefs, gradually shaping the modern-day Oruro Carnival. Its centrepiece is the Diablada — the Dance of Devils — during which revellers don elaborate demonic masks and costumes. pages.text: 7 Reasons to Visit San Antonio Now | National Geographic TRAVEL INTELLIGENT TRAVEL 7 Reasons to Visit San Antonio Now By Annie Fitzsimmons Published November 17, 2015 • 7 min read If your memories of San Antonio are limited to a stop at the Alamo and a meal on the River Walk accented by colorful umbrellas and mariachi music, it’s time to visit again. Texas’s second largest city is in the midst of a cultural revival, with the up-and-coming Pearl district leading the charge. With a burgeoning restaurant scene, historic restorations, and a raft of new construction, San Antonio is reinventing itself, becoming a multifaceted metropolis well worth exploring. Here are seven reasons you should visit now: 1. The River Walk Expansion San Antonio’s Paseo del Río remains its biggest draw. And though the below-street-level promenade continues to teem with tourists, major expansion efforts have thinned out the crowds and lured locals back downtown. The eight-mile Mission Reach extension, completed in 2013, connects four of the city’s five 18th-century frontier missions (excluding the Alamo) with walking and biking trails and restores the San Antonio River to its natural state. When combined with the previously completed Museum Reach segment, which connects the San Antonio Museum of Art to the Pearl neighborhood, the River Walk now encompasses a total of 15 miles—making the city’s cultural and historical offerings more accessible than ever. 2. At the southern tip of the African continent, it has landscapes ranging from beaches and bush to mountains and semi-deserts, a staggering array of flora and fauna and a multicultural population with 12 official languages. Cities such as Cape Town and Johannesburg may be obvious starting points, but it’s often the undiscovered corners that provide the most unforgettable experiences — from hiking among wild horses in Mpumalanga and watching hippos wander the streets of St Lucia to driving the historic mountain passes of the Karoo. Here are seven places worth considering for your next trip. Stellenbosch, Western Cape Best for: culture Beyond its famous winemaking heritage, which dates back to 1679, South Africa's second-oldest town is steeped in history and culture. Two meteor showers punctuate the month: The Draconids peak beneath the dark skies of a nearly new moon, while the Orionids arrive later in October. Saturn also reaches opposition, when the planet appears at its biggest and brightest, creating an excellent opportunity to glimpse its famed rings. Meteor showers—and, now that autumn has arrived, the northern lights —are best viewed beneath dark skies away from light pollution . But all is not lost for urban sky-watchers; some of the month’s top spectacles, including planet sightings, are visible through city lights. You just need to know when and where to look. Food cultures and practices are shaped by the landscape, the seasons and generations of know-how, whether it's foraging in mountain forests or harvesting the fruit of ancient trees. The ancient Egyptians saw it as a pool of cow’s milk, while in Hindu mythology the arcing galactic arm was likened to a dolphin swimming through the sky. Countless scientists, philosophers, and artists, including Galileo, Aristotle, and Vincent Van Gogh, have drawn upon the galaxy as their muse. Fabio Falchi, a researcher at the Light Pollution Science and Technology Institute (ISTIL) in Thiene, Italy, announced Friday the release of a new survey that quantifies nighttime sky quality for every region in the world. In every even-numbered year, the citizens who reside in each district can vote in an election to determine the representative of that district. The representative is a member of the House of Representatives, which is one of the two chambers of the Congress of the United States. Representatives hold great power, as they can propose and vote on bills that later can become laws. Each representative typically is affiliated with one of the two major political parties in the United States: the Democratic Party or the Republican Party. Each party naturally wants to ensure that they have as many representatives in Congress as possible. One way of achieving this is through gerrymandering

pages.description: The mysterious, silent giants face increasing threats in Africa. Relocating animals to create new populations could bolster some species but poses new risks.
pages.text: A bold plan to save Africa’s shrinking giraffe herds | National Geographic By Joshua Foer Photographs by Ami Vitale 25 min read This story appears in the October 2019 issue of National Geographic magazine. Of all the large African mammals that wildlife veterinarian Pete Morkel has had to capture over his career—lions, forest elephants, white rhinos— giraffes are the most stressful. “With other animals, you’re trying to give just enough anesthetic to immobilize them, but with a giraffe, we use a total overdose to chemically knock them off their feet,” the sun-leathered 59-year-old tells me as I stalk him stalking a two-year-old female giraffe somewhere in the Nigerien bush, about 60 miles east of Niamey, Niger’s capital. He is wearing a camo hat and a pair of torn, purple-checkered boxers that he’s been wearing as shorts for the past several days. ( Giraffes Seen Feasting on Skeleton—Here's Why) Morkel has loaded his dart gun with a dose of etorphine, an opioid about 6,000 times more powerful than morphine. Once it penetrates the giraffe’s skin, he and his team will have just minutes to chase down the animal, tackle her, and inject her neck with an antidote to keep her from dying. If she can be successfully captured and survive a 500-mile translocation across Niger, she’ll become one of eight founding “Adams” and “Eves” of a new population of one of the world’s rarest wild mammals. These items, which included buffalo robes, blankets, moccasins and a doll, had been taken from the Lakota community after the Blue Water Massacre in 1855 , the first major ambush on a Native American community by the U.S. Army. It would become the start of a decades-long campaign against the Plains tribes that would end with the death and displacement of numerous Native Americans. The return of the belongings offers a modicum of closure, but the pain of the massacre lives on among those on the reservation today. pages.description: Augustus was seen as a descendant of the gods who would go on to redefine authority. New research posits that his rule paved the way for Jesus
pages.text: A Cult Grew Around the First Emperor of Rome in 27 B.C. A New Book Argues His Followers Might Have Created the Template for Christianity Skip to main content This relief on a fourth-century sarcophagus from Gaul depicts scenes from the Bible, including the famous miracle of Christ multiplying the loaves (center). Public Domain How did the scattered followers of an itinerant preacher come to form the most populous religion in the world? Tim Whitmarsh—a classicist at the University of Cambridge and author of magisterial books about empire, the early novel and more—offers a compelling answer in his new book, Rome’s Age of Revolution: Augustus, Empire and the Making of Christianity. To wit, Christianity took much of its shape from the cult of Augustus, first emperor of Rome. The Augustan age saw a unique revolution that redefined authority, space and literature, remaking both the inner world and the outer. Augustus drew on centuries-old Roman prophecies to cast himself as the promised one . According to his propaganda, Italy experienced auguries and miracles at Augustus’ nativity; Augustus was declared a descendant of Rome’s mythical founder, Aeneas, and therefore of the gods, and he promised to renew Roman liberty from the decadence of the late Republic. As Whitmarsh writes: “The new world was presented as the fulfillment of all the best ideals of the old.” Just so, Jesus’s birth was claimed as the fulfillment of Old Testament prophecies about a coming emissary of God on Earth, and this novel form of monotheism was simultaneously cast as the fruition of the Hebrew faith. pages.text: A Guide to Big Bend National Park, Texas | National Geographic The Rio Grande and its tributaries run through southwest Texas' Big Bend National Park, one of the most remote national parks. Photograph by Inge Johnsson, Alamy TRAVEL Big Bend Hosts the Most Bird Species of Any National Park This remote Texas park is home to a remarkable diversity of life. Published November 5, 2009 • 3 min read Location: Texas Established: June 12, 1944 Size: 801,163 acres Chihuahuan Desert vegetation—bunchgrasses, creosote bushes, cactuses, lechuguillas, yuccas, sotols, and more—covers most of the terrain. But the Rio Grande and its lush floodplains and steep, narrow canyons form almost a park of their own. So do the Chisos Mountains; up to 20 degrees cooler than the desert floor, they harbor pine, juniper, and oak, as well as deer, mountain lions, bears, and other wildlife. A heavy rain transforms the desert: Normally dry creek beds roar with water, and seeds long dormant burst into fields of wildflowers. The rocks of Big Bend are a complex lot. Two seas, one after another, flowed and subsided in the region hundreds of millions of years ago, leaving thick deposits of limestone and shale. The present mountains, except the Chisos, uplifted along with the Rockies, roughly 75 million years ago. Around the same time, a 40-mile-wide trough—most of the present-day park—sank along fault lines, leaving the cliffs of Santa Elena Canyon to the west and the Sierra del Carmen to the east rising 1,500 feet and more above the desert floor. pages.text: A historic guide to San Marino | National Geographic Paid content for Visit San Marino By Julia Buckley Published June 4, 2026 Perched on the aptly named Monte Titano, or Mount Titan, the landlocked city-state of San Marino enjoys spectacular views. Everywhere you look, there’s 360-degree panoramas of the rolling hills of Emilia-Romagna and the Marche regions, cascading down to the Adriatic Sea. While the ravishing landscapes of this part of the peninsula haven’t changed, history has waged major upheaval: over the centuries, the surrounding regions have gone from independent states to occupied territories and, finally, a unified Italy. San Marino however, sat on its eyrie, has remained above the fray — one of Europe’s oldest (and smallest) republics, its borders haven’t changed since 1463. Visitors often include a visit to San Marino as part of a wider trip to Italy, but while curiosity is often what lures people up Monte Titano, it’s the remarkable history that makes them stay. Its warren of medieval streets blend Renaissance, early modern and 20th-century architecture, while a trio of towers top the mountain peak. Here’s how to navigate San Marino’s layers of proud history. San Marino's medieval streets look as though they've been untouched for centuries, with steep, winding alleys and tiny piazzas. Its sloped driveway leads to an attached garage. Pleasant eco-friendly landscaping, unassuming green-grey siding and classic-looking windows and doors all contribute to a sense of stately suburban normalcy. Scientists say the Kelvin wave could be dangerous for people—and deadly for wildlife—as it travels up the California coast. Last month, around 20 homes were evacuated in Long Beach, California after heavy surf caused flooding. A blob of warm water known as a Kelvin wave is exacerbating coastal flooding caused by warmer waters, storms, and rising seas. Mario Tama, Getty Images By Ruby Mellen Published October 6, 2026 Sea levels across the west coasts of the Americas are rising after a massive bulge of water, driven by wind changes and a warmer ocean, inched its way east along the equator and along the coasts. The phenomenon, called a Kelvin wave, has officials bracing for storm surges, erosion, and transformations in marine life. Networks of satellites and buoys across the ocean have been tracking the pulse of water, which arrived on Southern California’s coast last week and will continue north. Experts say that while the wave itself isn’t especially damaging to property or infrastructure along the coast, it can worsen the damage already being inflicted by an increase in storms, climate change-driven sea-level rise, and record-high ocean temperatures, which cause water to expand. It’s also one of the major signs that the much-anticipated super El Niño born in the equatorial Pacific Ocean has made it to North and South America. pages.text: A new species offers a clue to the boom of giant dinosaurs | National Geographic SCIENCE A new species offers a clue to the boom of giant dinosaurs Nagatitan chaiyaphumensis may be the largest dinosaur ever found in Southeast Asia. Paleontologists estimate this behemoth weighed 30 tons and measured over 88 feet long. The recent discovery of Nagatitan chaiyaphumensis , shown in this illustration, in Thailand adds support to the idea that warm, open, and relatively dry habitats created ideal conditions for the evolution of giant sauropods. DinoThaiThai By Riley Black Published May 14, 2026 Titans once towered over Thailand. A research team led by National Geographic Explorer Sita Manitkoon has discovered a new long-necked dinosaur they estimate was over 88 feet long and weighed nearly 30 tons. “Initial measurements of the bones excavated suggested that this could be the largest dinosaur ever found in Southeast Asia,” says Manitkoon, a paleontologist at Mahasarakham University in Thailand. The telltale bones were uncovered in 2016 by a local man named Thanom Luangnan in Chaiyaphum Province, northeastern Thailand. “He observed what he described as strange-looking rocks on the banks of a public pond,” says Manitkoon. Luangnan reported the findings to the country’s Department of Mineral Resources. The strange rocks, it turned out, were dinosaur bones, and when Manitkoon came upon them, he knew the creature must have been enormous. He made lasting reforms to all aspects of royal power, from the organization of the justice system to economic reform, and revived culture along classical lines. Island-hopping is a charming way to discover Croatia, allowing you to enjoy shots of espresso and shimmering sea views on deck as you sail from coast to coast. National ferry operator Jadrolinija and private competitors link most inhabited islands in the country. National company Jadrolinija operates car-ferries and passenger-only catamarans throughout the islands, which are supplemented by vessels run by private operators such as Kapetan Luka. While the moon won’t actually appear blue, the combination highlights an unusual overlap between the lunar cycle and the moon’s orbit around Earth. The full moon reaches peak illumination at 8:45 a.m. UTC on May 31, offering skywatchers a chance to catch one of the year’s more unusual lunar events. The moon may appear slightly smaller and dimmer than a typical full moon, though binoculars or photography can help reveal the subtle differences. There are actually two accepted definitions of a blue moon. The most widely known is a monthly blue moon, which is a second full moon in a calendar month. Intent on seeing the work at each booth, people slowly make their way through the room to appreciate jewelry made from tiny Niihau shells , lauhala hats with woven hala leaves, carved koa bowls, aloha wear and some of the finest Hawaiian featherwork. While a highlight of the annual Merrie Monarch Festival in Hilo is its internationally acclaimed hula competition, the central purpose of the weeklong spring event is the perpetuation, preservation and promotion of Hawaiian culture. More than 150 Hawaiian Islands artisans display their works at the fair, and even more are spread throughout the city in pop-up makeke (markets) that showcase traditional and modern work. pages.description: In 1990, National Geographic went to the Soviet Union to report on one of the worst environmental disasters of the 20th century: the shrinking of the Aral Sea.
pages.text: A Soviet sea, killed by an obsession with 'white gold' | National Geographic Premium ENVIRONMENT FROM THE VAULT A Soviet sea, killed by an obsession with 'white gold' In 1990, National Geographic went to the Soviet Union to report on one of the worst environmental disasters of the 20th century: the shrinking of the Aral Sea. From the rusting deck of the boat he captained for years, Dzhetpisbai Ibragimov surveys a sandy waste once part of the great Aral Sea. By William S. Ellis Photographs by David C. Turnley Published April 21, 2026 This story originally published in the February 1990 issue of National Geographic magazine. See more digitized stories from our archives here . The mighty inland sea lies stricken now, caught in the grip of some evil chemistry as its waters dry to salt and blow away as noxious dust to strike the people with illness and death. It has never happened before within the time frame of a single generation, the disappearance of such a large body of water; but the Soviet Union's Aral Sea, once larger in area than any of the Great Lakes save Superior, is vanishing from the face of the earth. As the waters continue to recede, final destruction of the Aral—26,000 square miles in 1960—could occur before another 30 years have passed. The desiccation is taking place not only at a rapid pace but also with stealth, and in silence: the way a stallion plunges his muzzle into a bucket of water and drains it. Photograph: Smith Collection/Gado/Getty Images El Niño southern oscillation A super El Niño brings startling changes for marine life on California coast: ‘Like nothing we’ve ever seen’ Water temperatures are climbing the charts, high tides are swallowing the shoreline and vital parts of the food web that feed ocean diversity are disappearing Gabrielle Canon in Monterey Bay, California Fri 13 Nov 2026 07.00 EST Last modified on Tue 17 Nov 2026 16.50 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google On a picturesque autumn afternoon last week, the beaches of California ’s Monterey Bay were teeming with life and death. A cadre of shorebirds charged and retreated in a synchronized dance with the raging surf. Nearby, the receding tides had deposited lifeless bundles of feathers and bone, tangled in piles of glistening kelp. Swollen sea lion carcasses, their teeth bared in a quiet grimace, dotted the sand as beach picnickers and dog walkers enjoyed the warm, cloudless day. The effects of a historic El Niño have officially reached Monterey Bay , according to scientists, and the mortality on display here may be a grim harbinger of more to come.
